passage:
On Afreen's last afternoon at the district health office, she handed Ishita a thick folder. "The vaccination camp registrations are yours now. It's all in there."
Ishita opened it but didn't let her go yet. "Can I say back what I think I own? From Monday I collect the village lists from the health workers, enter them by Thursday, and send the final count to the camp doctor."
"Yes, exactly."
"What's not in the folder? Anything half-done?"
Afreen paused. "Oh. Kharkhoda sent their list on paper, not by email. It's in my drawer, not entered yet. And the doctor prefers a phone call if the count changes after Thursday."
Ishita wrote both on a sticky note and stuck it to the laptop. "Anyone I should call if I get stuck?"
"Suresh in accounts knows the old sheets."
Ishita read all three points back once more. Afreen laughed. "You've just saved me three worried phone calls next week."

qa.q: Where was the Kharkhoda list?
qa.a: It was on paper in Afreen's drawer, not entered yet.

qa.q: What might Afreen have felt when Ishita asked what was not in the folder?
qa.a: Afreen seemed briefly caught off guard, pausing before remembering the paper list, and then relieved, laughing that Ishita had saved three worried phone calls.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's questions did the most good, and why?
qa.a: "What's not in the folder? Anything half-done?" brought out the paper list and the doctor's preference while Afreen was still there to ask.

qa.q: What would change if Ishita had just said "Okay, thanks" and taken the folder?
qa.a: The Kharkhoda list might have sat unentered in the drawer, the count could have been wrong, and next week would have meant confusion and chasing Afreen.

grounding: Shows a receiver repeating back what they now own and asking what is missing before the person handing over leaves.

passage:
Okay, Kalyani, don't laugh. Remember Thursday, when I finished the physics worksheet in fifteen minutes? I was so proud. Cricket was starting at six on the colony ground and I wanted to bat first. So I zipped through: wrote the formulas, plugged in numbers, didn't check units, didn't read question seven properly. Done. Out the door.
Today Sir gave them back. Eleven out of twenty. In question three I wrote force in kilograms. Question seven asked for time and I gave speed. The worst part? I knew all of it. Sir circled the answers and wrote, "You know this. Slow down." Now I have to redo the whole sheet by Monday, so those fifteen minutes have turned into an evening. And I got out for four runs anyway. That's me, Gurpreet, the fastest finisher in class ten, with the marks to show for it.

qa.q: What score did Gurpreet get on the worksheet?
qa.a: Eleven out of twenty.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel on Thursday compared with today?
qa.a: On Thursday Gurpreet felt proud and eager to get to cricket; today Gurpreet feels frustrated and a bit embarrassed, since every answer was within reach.

qa.q: What small step could Gurpreet take before rushing out next time?
qa.a: Spend a couple of minutes rereading each question and checking the units before closing the book.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Gurpreet's worksheet?
qa.a: The teacher sees someone who knows the work but rushed it, which is why the note says "You know this. Slow down."

grounding: Shows a teenager hurrying through homework to get to play, making careless errors that cost marks and a redo.

passage:
Writing centre notes, 12 March. Student: Keerthana, second-year history.
Third session on the same essay introduction. She brought six printed versions of page one, each with tiny changes: "crucial" swapped for "vital", a comma moved, one sentence shifted to the end and then back. The body of the essay is still blank. The deadline is Friday.
When I asked what would happen if she sent a rough draft to her professor for comments, she went very still and said, "Then he'll know I'm not good at this." She also mentioned skipping badminton practice twice this week "to get the opening right".
What I did: set a timer for twenty-five minutes and asked her to write the next section badly on purpose, no deleting. She wrote a full page. Her hands were shaking at first.
Plan: meet Thursday. Page one is frozen until the body exists.
Damini, writing centre

qa.q: How many printed versions of page one did Keerthana bring?
qa.a: She brought six printed versions of page one.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana go very still when asked about sending a rough draft?
qa.a: She seemed afraid of being judged, believing a rough draft would show her professor that she is "not good at this".

qa.q: Which of Damini's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking Keerthana to write the next section badly on purpose, on a timer with no deleting, got a full page written and moved her past the frozen opening.

qa.q: How might Damini feel watching Keerthana's hands shake as she wrote?
qa.a: Damini was likely concerned at how much fear sat behind the rewriting, and encouraged that a full page came once deleting was off the table.

grounding: Shows a student rewriting one page over and over, unable to submit anything imperfect, while fear of criticism steals time.

passage:
Mohit, before you hit submit on that internship application, let me tell you about my checklist. In first year I emailed a cover letter to a firm in Chennai that began "Dear Hiring Team at" followed by the name of a totally different company. I'd copied it from my previous application. They never replied. I didn't blame them.
So now I, Naveen, never send anything important without four checks. One: every name. Is it theirs, spelt right? Two: every number: dates, marks, phone. Three: attachments. Actually attached, and the right version, not "CV_old". Four: I reopen their original message and tick off everything they asked for. Takes two minutes, maybe three.
Last month it caught a wrong date on my scholarship form and a missing transcript. Nobody saw those mistakes except me, and that's the whole point. Okay, now open yours and read me their original email.

qa.q: Which four things does Naveen check before sending?
qa.a: Every name, every number, the attachments, and the original message's list of what they asked for.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the first-year cover letter?
qa.a: Naveen felt embarrassed and didn't blame the firm for not replying, since the letter named a totally different company.

qa.q: What could Mohit do right now, before submitting?
qa.a: Mohit could reopen the internship's original email and tick off each item, then check the names, numbers and that the right attachments are there.

qa.q: How might the firm in Chennai have seen Naveen's letter?
qa.a: They probably saw it as careless copying, since it opened with another company's name, and simply didn't reply.

grounding: Shows a careful person using a short checklist of names, numbers, attachments and the original request before submitting.

passage:
"Rashmi, the morning copy took me an hour again," Indu said, dropping into the chair beside her. "Forty bookings, all by hand."
"I know, I know. That was meant to be temporary."
"Since when?"
Rashmi checked her notebook. "Since March. The booking form stopped talking to the sheet the week of the big sale. I pasted the bookings over myself and said I'd fix the link properly after the rush."
"It's November."
"There was always another rush." Rashmi rubbed her forehead. "And then Arjun built the invoice sheet on top of my pasted columns. So if I fix the link now, the invoices break."
"So two things to fix."
"Three. The reminder messages read from the same columns."
Indu was quiet for a moment. "Can you block one afternoon? I'll cover the phones."
"Friday," Rashmi said. "Write it on the board so I can't wriggle out."

qa.q: When did the booking form stop connecting to the sheet?
qa.a: In March, the week of the big sale.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Indu pointed out it was November?
qa.a: Rashmi felt guilty and weary, rubbing her forehead, because a fix promised for after the rush had grown into three tangled problems.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The quick patch was never given a real slot and others built on top of it; blocking Friday afternoon, with Indu on the phones and the plan on the board, gives the fix a real time.

qa.q: What is the patch like for Indu every morning?
qa.a: For Indu it means an hour of copying forty bookings by hand, a daily cost of a shortcut Indu never chose.

grounding: Shows a worker's hurried patch, meant to be fixed later, becoming permanent and piling up work for others.

passage:
Friday, late.
Thirty chairs went out today. Same four of us, same one spray booth, ten more chairs than last week. On Monday Elizabeth said, "The client needs them Friday, just make it work." So we made it work. Second coat of varnish on the seats only, not the legs. Coarse sandpaper, because the fine one takes twice as long.
I kept thinking of Papa's rule in his old workshop: never let a chair leave that you wouldn't sit on. I wouldn't sit on these for long.
At four, a call came about last week's batch: sticky arms, a rough edge. Elizabeth came to the booth and asked, "Who finished these?" Not what happened. Who.
Nobody mentioned Monday. I said nothing either. I'm writing it here instead, which feels like its own kind of hiding. Next week, before we start, I want to tell her how many hours a proper finish really takes.
Rehana

qa.q: How many chairs went out on Friday?
qa.a: Thirty chairs went out today, ten more than last week.

qa.q: What is Rehana feeling about the chairs that went out?
qa.a: Rehana feels torn and uneasy because the chairs break Papa's rule, and ashamed of staying silent when Elizabeth asked who finished them.

qa.q: What could Rehana say to Elizabeth next week, and when?
qa.a: Before work starts, Rehana could tell Elizabeth plainly how many hours a proper finish takes for that many chairs, so the trade-off is decided openly.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth seem to see the sticky chairs?
qa.a: Elizabeth seems to treat them as someone's careless finishing, asking "Who" rather than linking them to Monday's push for more chairs with the same team.

grounding: Shows staff pushed to deliver more with the same resources, torn between their standards and the demand and quietly blamed for defects.

passage:
Two days before the school sports day, Hafsa found Nikita in the staffroom with a list split into two columns.
"Why is 'banner' in the right column?" Hafsa asked. "You redid it three times last year."
"Exactly," Nikita said. "Nobody remembered the banner. The left column is what must be perfect. First-aid table staffed all day, water every hundred metres, the long-jump pit raked and checked for stones. And the engraved medals: once a name is cut into metal, we can't undo it, so the list gets checked twice, by two people."
"And the right column?"
"Certificates, decorations, the music list. Good enough is fine. If a certificate prints off-centre, we reprint one."
Hafsa read the medal list slowly while Nikita checked the first-aid box. They found one misspelled name, Tejaswini with an 'i' missing.
On the day, the banner sagged a little. Nobody got hurt, and every medal was right.

qa.q: What mistake did Hafsa find on the medal list?
qa.a: A misspelled name: Tejaswini with an 'i' missing.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa be puzzled about where the banner is listed?
qa.a: Hafsa seems surprised and puzzled, since Nikita redid the banner three times last year yet now puts it in the good-enough column.

qa.q: How did Nikita decide which things got extra care?
qa.a: Nikita gave extra care to what affects safety or can't be undone, like first aid, water, the pit and the engraved names, and let decorations be good enough.

qa.q: What would change if the medal list had not been checked twice?
qa.a: A student might have been handed a medal with a misspelled name cut into the metal, a mistake that cannot be undone.

grounding: Shows a worker choosing which parts need real care, like safety and things hard to undo, and letting the rest be good enough.

passage:
In the small kitchen of their Kolkata flat, Himani reached for the steel glass and it tipped. Milk ran across the table and dripped onto the floor. Himani froze, then slid under the table and pulled her knees up tight.
Her mother, Urmila, came in and saw the puddle. She took a slow breath. "Himani, milk spills. Come, we'll clean it together."
Slowly Himani crawled out. Urmila handed her the small cloth and took the big one. They wiped side by side until the floor shone.
"All gone," Himani whispered, and smiled a little.

qa.q: Where did Himani go after the milk spilled?
qa.a: She slid under the table and pulled her knees up tight.

qa.q: Why might Himani have hidden under the table?
qa.a: Himani was probably scared that her mother would be angry about the spilled milk.

qa.q: What did Urmila do that helped Himani?
qa.a: Urmila stayed calm, said milk spills, and cleaned up side by side with Himani, giving her a small cloth of her own.

qa.q: What would change if Urmila had shouted?
qa.a: Himani might have stayed hidden and learned that mistakes are shameful, instead of learning they can be cleaned up and fixed.

grounding: Shows a young child freezing and hiding after a spill, and a calm clean-up together showing the mistake can be fixed.

passage:
During wet break in their Kraków classroom, Olga tossed a rubber ball to Thabo and it hit the globe on the teacher's desk. The globe rolled off, and a crack split right across the Atlantic.
Pan Nowak came back and stared at it. "Who did this?"
Olga's stomach went tight. Last month he had made Kuba stand in the corridor the whole afternoon for spilling paint. "It was already cracked," she said. "It was like that this morning."
Thabo looked at the floor and said nothing.
Pan Nowak frowned but moved on to spelling. Olga didn't hear a single word of the lesson. On the bus home, Thabo said quietly, "You didn't have to say that." Olga pressed her forehead against the cold window and didn't answer.

qa.q: What happened to the globe?
qa.a: It rolled off the desk and a crack split right across the Atlantic.

qa.q: Why did Olga say the globe was already cracked?
qa.a: Olga was scared of being punished, remembering that Pan Nowak made Kuba stand in the corridor all afternoon for spilling paint.

qa.q: What could make it easier for Olga to tell the truth next time?
qa.a: If Pan Nowak met accidents calmly, for example by asking who could help fix things rather than punishing, Olga might feel safe enough to own up.

qa.q: What is it like for Thabo when Olga blames the globe's crack on the morning?
qa.a: Thabo seems uncomfortable and torn, staring at the floor in class and later saying quietly, "You didn't have to say that."

grounding: Shows a schoolchild lying about a breakage out of fear of a harsh punishment seen earlier.

passage:
Coach's notes, under-16 hockey, Wednesday.
Nirmala has not taken a single penalty corner in practice since Saturday's final, where her flick went wide and we lost 1–0. Today, when I called her name for the drill, she said she had a headache and sat on the bench retying the same lace. Her friend told me she has watched the match video "maybe twenty times" and keeps saying, "I'm the reason we lost."
After practice I sat next to her. I told her I missed two strokes in a state final at her age and still remember the smell of the grass. She almost smiled. I said one flick is one flick, not the whole player.
Next steps: tomorrow she takes five flicks at an empty goal, no keeper, only me watching. I've messaged her mother that it has been a hard week, so home knows to go gently.
Rukmini

qa.q: What was the result of Saturday's final?
qa.a: They lost 1–0 after Nirmala's flick went wide.

qa.q: What does Nirmala retying the same lace suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels ashamed and afraid of missing again, avoiding the drill because she sees herself as "the reason we lost".

qa.q: Why might five flicks at an empty goal help Nirmala?
qa.a: It lets her try again in a small, low-pressure way with only the coach watching, so one miss can stop feeling like a verdict on her.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see Nirmala's miss?
qa.a: Rukmini sees it as one flick, not the whole player, remembering missing two strokes in a state final at the same age.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a visible error for days and avoiding trying again, and a coach helping her restart.
